tone_statements.citation: Liao Hanbo 廖漢波. 2016. Tonal development of Tai languages. MA thesis (Linguistics), Payap University, Chiang Mai (approved 31 May 2016; advisor Phinnarat Akharawatthanakun). xxii+426 pp. (448 PDF pages). [Appendix C, Language 36: Yizhou Suogan, Guibei Zhuang, pp. 399-403 (first-hand, 2 LRPs, May 2013); Language 38: Donglan, Guibei Zhuang, pp. 407-408 (after Zhang et al. 1999)].
tone_statements.quote: 36.4 Tonal characteristics & tone occurrences: six distinct tones. Tone 1: High-falling 51 occurs in A[1-A, 1-C, 1-U, 1-UC, 1-G] ... as well as a higher level 55 occurs in DS[1-A, 1-C, 1-U, 1-UC, 1-G] ... Tone 2: Low-rising-falling 231 occurs in A [2, 1/2] ... Tone 3: High level 33 ... Tone 4: Low-level 11 occurs in B[2, 1/2], Tone 5: High-falling 42 ... Tone 6: Low-rising 24 occurs in C[2, 1/2]. 36.5 Phonation types or voice qualities of tones in this dialect. A1 (51) has a creakiness triggered by its rapid falling contour from the highest pitch 5 to the lowest pitch 1; B2 (11) also accompanies a weak creakiness due to the lowest pitch; C2 has a glottal constriction ... All these voice qualities are not phonemic.
tone_statements.locator: Appendix C, Language 36 (Yizhou Suogan, Guibei Zhuang), §36.4–36.5, p. 401
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

sources.note: Suogan Guibei Zhuang has six distinct tones on smooth syllables — 51 (A1, creaky), 231 (A2), 33 (B1), 11 (B2, weakly creaky), 42 (C1), 24ˀ (C2, glottal constriction) — with checked-syllable values 55 (DS1), 33 (DL1) and 23 (D2) treated as allotones; phonation differences are non-phonemic; a unique partial split in the proto-voiced row (items from *mw-, *nr-/*C̬.n-, *g(l)- taking upper-register tones, shared with Huanjiang) motivates a separate 'Guibei Zhuang tone box' (ch. 6); Donglan (L38, after Zhang et al. 1999) likewise has six tones: 53/55, 231, 35, 11, 33, 14.
